summary: Solid, sourced, family-friendly core exists. Two real trees of the Yucatan forest: the chechen (Metopium brownei, black poisonwood) has caustic sap that burns and blisters skin, and the chaca (Bursera simaruba, gumbo-limbo, red peeling bark) often grows near it and is the traditional remedy (documented in UADY and CICY academic publications as a Maya-area folk remedy, with no clinical trial found). The dominant legend (about a dozen Spanish/English retellings agree): two warrior-prince brothers, Kinich (kind, younger) and Tizic (proud, harsh, elder), both love Nicte-Ha; their rivalry ends in a duel and both die; the gods grant their wish to be near her / to return and turn them into two trees that must stay together: Tizic becomes the chechen (harm), Kinich the chaca (cure). Moral: where there is poison, the cure is close by; opposites are kept in balance. A rarer variant has a cruel king Chechen and a kind princess Chaca(h) whose trees grow from their graves. Recommended beginner-story core: forest, two trees, two brothers, gods turn them into trees that stand together, chechen burns / chaca heals, 'if you see a chechen, a chaca is near'. Keep deaths and the duel soft or implicit; do not give medical instructions.
facts: The chechen is Metopium brownei (Jacq.) Urb., family Anacardiaceae (the cashew / poison-ivy family); English name black poisonwood; also written chechem or chechen. Sources: en.wikipedia Metopium_brownei; UADY Revista Biomedica 2001; Posta.

The chaca is Bursera simaruba (L.) Sarg., family Burseraceae; English name gumbo-limbo; also called tourist tree (red, sunburn-like peeling bark) and, in Spanish, palo mulato. Sources: en.wikipedia Bursera_simaruba; CICY Desde el Herbario 8; Chamlaty.

Chechen contains urushiol, the oily irritant of the poison-ivy family; contact with its sap, bark or leaves can cause painful contact dermatitis (redness, itching, blisters). Sources: en.wikipedia Metopium_brownei; Por Esto 2025; Posta; Muy Interesante; yucalandia.

Academic (UADY, Rev Biomed 2001;12:86-96, Flores, Canto-Aviles, Flores-Serrano): Metopium brownei, Maya name written 'Che che'en', is on the list of toxic plants of the Yucatan flora; latex of stem and leaves; found in dune scrub and medium/low forest; its leaves give off volatile substances that cause burns on the body; allergic people can react even when standing away from the trees, so one should avoid its shade.

The chechen's sap turns black on contact with air, so the trunk often shows black blotches or streaks; the bark is scaly or pale with dark spots. Sources: Por Esto 2025; Muy Interesante; Chamlaty; yucalandia.
The chechen is a tall, straight tree, commonly cited as reaching about 25 m (Chamlaty: 12-25 m); its wood is valued as lumber. Sources: Posta; Por Esto; Chamlaty; Wikipedia.
Range of the chechen: Yucatan Peninsula to Veracruz (Mexico), Belize, northern Guatemala, Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica; IUCN Least Concern. Source: en.wikipedia Metopium_brownei.

The chaca has reddish-brown bark that peels naturally in thin papery scales, showing a greenish layer beneath; it reaches up to about 15 m. Sources: Muy Interesante; Posta; CICY (papery scales, up to 15 m); Wikipedia.
The chaca is native to the Yucatan Peninsula and widespread there in evergreen and deciduous forest and in secondary growth (CICY, Desde el Herbario 8, 2016, David Castillo Acal).

CICY (Centro de Investigacion Cientifica de Yucatan) states, citing Cabrera Cano & Sanchez Vazquez 2000 (Etnoflora Yucatanense 16, Universidad Autonoma de Yucatan), that in the Maya area chakaj is used as a remedy for the burn produced by contact with the 'chechen negro' (Metopium brownei).

UADY Rev Biomed 2001 says: after contact with the resin of Che che'en, a bath prepared with bark and leaves of the tree called Chacah (Bursera simaruba) is recommended; it acts as the antidote and prevents burns from appearing.

The remedy is described differently by different sources: bath of bark and leaves (UADY); wash, tea or ointment from the sap under the bark (Por Esto); crushed or mashed leaves applied to the skin (Muy Interesante, De Peso Yucatan, Yucatan Today); resin or 'nectar' in the legend tellings. The consistent point is that chaca (bark, leaves or sap) is the folk remedy.

The chechen and chaca are often found growing near each other (Muy Interesante: they often grow together; Por Esto: chaka is sometimes found near chechen; Conrad: gumbo-limbo grows near poisonwood in most areas). mayan.org adds that they do NOT always grow together and that the legend highlights the cases where they do.

Core legend (consistent across nearly all retellings): two opposite figures, one harsh and harmful, one kind and healing, end up as two trees that stay close; the harmful one is the chechen, the healing one is the chaca; the meaning is poison and cure side by side, balance of opposites (Posta, Culturagenial, mayan.org, El Automata, Yucatan Today).

Dominant version: princes/warrior brothers Kinich (younger, kind, loved by the people) and Tizic (older, arrogant, ruthless) both love Nicte-Ha, fight to the death over her, and the gods turn them into trees (Tizic = chechen, Kinich = chaca) that must stay together forever (Posta, Culturagenial, mayan.org, Yucatan Today, De Peso, Muy Interesante, Wikipedia).

In the retellings, wherever a chechen grows a chaca is said to grow nearby ('si encuentras un chechen, pronto encuentras un chacah' - Culturagenial; 'detras de un chechen siempre hay un Chacah' - Tierras Mayas).
Several retellings describe the sky darkening and the moon hiding during the brothers' fight because the gods were angered (Culturagenial, De Peso, Descubro).
The Maya healers called h-men (H'menes) were among the people interviewed by the UADY toxic-plants survey in 25 Maya communities (300 interviews), the basis of the Che che'en entry.
variants: Version A (dominant, about a dozen sources): brothers Kinich and Tizic + Nicte-Ha. Kinich younger and kind, Tizic older and arrogant (Posta). Duel to the death; the gods turn them into trees. Tizic = chechen, Kinich = chaca. Sources: Posta, Culturagenial, mayan.org, Yucatan Today, De Peso, Muy Interesante, El Automata, NicteHa.love, Wikipedia.

A1, what the brothers ask the gods: in the underworld they ask to return and see Nicte-Ha once more; the gods agree on condition they come back together and stay near each other (Posta, Yucatan Today). In mayan.org and El Automata the gods are simply 'moved by the tragedy' and turn them into trees so they stand together forever.

A2, Nicte-Ha's fate differs: unspecified (Posta); had already died of sadness before they returned (Muy Interesante); becomes a white water lily, Nymphaea ampla (mayan.org); becomes the trees' shared flower (Wikipedia); dies of sorrow and is reborn as a white flower by the water / lirio (De Peso, Descubro). No consensus.
A3, who she loves: mayan.org says Nicte-Ha chooses Kinich and jealous Tizic then challenges him; most others say only that both love her and fight.

A4, side details in only one source: the gods darken the sky and hide the moon (Culturagenial, De Peso); Tizic made a pact with the underworld (NicteHa.love, one of two options); a farmer from Oxkutzcab saved by a warrior figure who is Kinich (De Peso, modern anecdote).

Version B (rarer): not brothers. A cruel Maya king Chechen is overthrown and killed by his people and swears revenge; a poisonous tree grows from his grave. A kind princess Chaca(h) dies young and is buried beside him so her goodness keeps his ghost away; the healing chaca grows there. Sources: Tierras Mayas (which itself contradicts this in a summary box with two brothers) and Chamlaty (2015). Ending shared with A: where a chechen grows, a chaca grows nearby.

Version C (generic): two brothers of opposite character, no named woman: Chechen (hate, resentment) and Chaka (kind, generous); a dispute ends in their deaths and the gods turn them into trees (Por Esto 2025).

Setting: the Yucatan Peninsula in general (Posta, mayan.org); Quintana Roo jungle in Muy Interesante and El Momento Quintana Roo (not fetched). No village-specific attribution found in any reachable source.
Spelling of the characters varies: Kinich / Kinch (Wikipedia, NicteHa.love), Tizic / Tizik (Muy Interesante lead), Nicte-Ha / Nicte Ha / Nicte-Ha.

maya_terms.meaning: Maya-derived name of the black poisonwood tree, Metopium brownei. 'Che che'en' is the form in the UADY toxic-plants paper; 'Chechem' per Yucatan Today and Wikipedia; 'chechén' is the Spanish-press form most used in the legend.

maya_terms.term: chacá (also chaká, chacáh, chacah, chakah, chakaj, chaka)
maya_terms.meaning: Maya-derived name of the gumbo-limbo, Bursera simaruba, red peeling bark. 'Chakaj' per CICY and Yucatan Today; 'Chacah' per UADY; 'chacá' is the Spanish-press form used in most legend tellings. Other Yucatan names listed by CICY: chacah colorado, chakack, chakchakh, huk'up, sakchakah. CICY (citing Cabrera & Sanchez 2000) says 'chacah' suggests 'el casposo' (scaly) or 'gomoso/resinoso' (gummy/resinous).
Name of the kind younger brother who becomes the chaca. Meaning of the name not given in any fetched source; do not state an etymology.
Name of the proud older brother who becomes the chechen. Meaning not given in fetched sources.

The young woman both brothers love. NicteHa.love glosses the name as 'flor blanca' (white flower); the same name is used in a separate legend (prince Chaktzitzib, sacred cenote, water lily and cardinal), which is a different story.
Traditional Maya healers/knowledge holders; the UADY survey interviewed them about toxic plants. Useful only as a background term.
Spanish common name for Bursera simaruba (Chamlaty).
White flower of the water (water lily), in some versions the form Nicte-Ha takes; 'sac nicté' is the white flower associated with her in NicteHa.love.
Spanish words used in every retelling: poison / antidote / sap / bark. Good beginner vocabulary for the story.

cautions: Do not present the chaca as a proven cure. The remedy is documented as a Maya-area folk remedy (CICY citing Etnoflora Yucatanense 2000; UADY 2001), but no clinical trial was found, Wikipedia tags it 'citation needed', and Jim Conrad reports villagers in Yokdzonot mostly used bitter-orange juice instead. Phrase it as 'people say / the legend says / tradition says'.

Do not give first-aid or treatment instructions or tell children to touch either tree. Keep the safe message: do not touch the chechen; if skin is hurt, tell an adult / see a doctor (Posta and Yucatan Today both stress medical care for serious symptoms).

No ethnographic primary source (INAH, UNAM, Secretaria de Cultura, published folklore collection) for the Kinich/Tizic version was found; the earliest dated retelling reachable was Chamlaty 2015 and most others are 2020s press/blog pieces, some possibly AI-assisted. Call it 'a legend told in Yucatan', not 'an ancient Maya myth recorded in the villages'. Do not claim a specific village origin.

mayan.org (the most 'authoritative-looking' page) cites Caceres 1995 and others and claims centuries of j-men poultices; those citations and claims were not verified and should not be repeated. Its claims about rain dripping from leaves burning people and chechen/chaca sharing habitat are also single-source (Tierras Mayas repeats the rain claim).

Death and violence: the brothers fight to the death over a woman, and in several versions Nicte-Ha dies of sadness. For a beginner family-friendly story, omit the duel and deaths, e.g. 'the brothers quarrelled over Nicte-Ha, the gods were sad and turned them into two trees'. Do not state Nicte-Ha's fate (no consensus).

Religion: 'the gods' (plural, unnamed) and an underworld appear in the legend; keep to 'the gods' without naming specific Maya deities, and avoid asserting beliefs. Do not mention Tizic's pact with the underworld (single source).
Do not mix in the separate Nicte-Ha legend (prince Chaktzitzib / Chacdziedzib, sacred cenote, water lily and cardinal bird); it is a different story that happens to share the woman's name.

Spelling is not standardized (chechén/chechem/Che che'en; chacá/chaká/chacáh/chakaj). Pick one set for the story (suggest chechén and chacá, the forms in most Spanish retellings and in the original request) and mention the others once if needed.

Which brother is older, and whether Nicte-Ha chose one, differ by source; do not state who is older unless needed (Posta: Kinich younger, Tizic older). Do not give etymologies for Kinich or Tizic; none were verified.

Keep geography general ('the forests of Yucatan'); Quintana Roo/Bacalar attributions come from single press pieces. Atlas Obscura returned 403 and Informe Fracto had an expired certificate, so they were not read directly.
The 'tourist tree' nickname refers to the bark looking like sunburnt skin and was not found as a Maya term; it is optional trivia only.
